extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent prosecutors and patent attorneys handling USPTO examination and PTAB matters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for overcoming an obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103) rejection by attacking the examiner’s prima facie case during U.S. patent prosecution (and analogously in PTAB proceedings). Focuses on litigation- and prosecution-oriented arguments tied to MPEP and Federal Circuit/Supreme Court precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case burden allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO bears the initial burden of establishing a prima facie case of obviousness; if the examiner fails to establish a prima facie case the applicant need not submit rebuttal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2142: examiner must factually support any prima facie conclusion; if no prima facie case is made, applicant need not rebut. In PTAB proceedings burden allocation differs (petitioner has initial burden) but the same lack-of-presumption concept applies. Cite In re Oetiker, In re Piasecki, In re Rinehart.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for obviousness (A: combining elements to predictable results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results is a recognized obviousness rationale under MPEP § 2143.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to identify examiner rationale and to craft counter-arguments about predictability/unexpected results; consult cases reviewed in MPEP § 2143(I).

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for obviousness (B: simple substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results is a recognized obviousness rationale under MPEP § 2143.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examiner relies on substitution, challenge predictability, show non-interchangeability or unexpected results, or show lack of motivation to substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for obviousness (C: known technique to improve similar devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way is a recognized obviousness rationale under MPEP § 2143.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue differences in context, lack of reasonable expectation of success, or that prior art teaches away from such an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for obviousness (D: applying known technique to a known device ready for improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results is a recognized obviousness rationale under MPEP § 2143.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the device was not 'ready for improvement', that modification would render it inoperable, or that no motivation existed to apply the technique for the asserted purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for obviousness (E: obvious-to-try with finite predictable options)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Obvious to try”—choosing from a finite number of identified predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success—is an MPEP/KSR obviousness rationale (post-KSR context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cases where numerous unpredictable choices existed; emphasize unpredictability or lack of reasonable expectation of success to rebut an 'obvious to try' theory. See KSR and Eisai v. Dr. Reddy’s.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for obviousness (F: known work in one field prompting predictable variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field may prompt variations for use in same or different fields based on design incentives or market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue lack of cross-field analogy, lack of suggestion to adapt the teaching to the other field, or unpredictable results across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP rationales for obviousness (G: teaching, suggestion, or motivation in prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine references to arrive at the claimed invention is a recognized rationale (MPEP § 2143(I)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge the asserted motivation to combine by showing no such teaching/suggestion/motivation exists in the prior art or that it is derived from hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection is conclusory and relies on 'common sense' (insufficient reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner’s obviousness rejection that is conclusory or relies solely on unspecified 'common sense' or 'common knowledge' without articulated reasoning is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue the rejection is unsupported; require the examiner to 'set forth its findings and the grounds' with evidentiary support. Cite KSR, In re Lee, In re Zurko, In re Nuvasive, TriMed v. Stryker. Show that 'common sense' cannot substitute for reasoned analysis or authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to consider the totality of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must consider the totality of the record, including applicant’s rebuttal evidence and any objective/secondary considerations, rather than relying solely on the prior conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the examiner did not weigh rebuttal evidence or secondary considerations; cite MPEP §§ 2141(II), 2145, In re Eli Lilly, TriMed v. Stryker, and In re Chu. Emphasize that rebuttal evidence must be evaluated along with the facts that led to the initial rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to undertake a full Graham analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper obviousness determination must analyze all four Graham factors: scope and content of the prior art; differences between the prior art and the claims; level of ordinary skill in the art; and relevant secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge any faulty or incomplete Graham analysis. Under KSR the four factors are not alternatives — all must be analyzed. Use cases (Kinetic Concepts, Vicor) and MPEP § 2141.1; ensure examiner applies analogous-art tests and considers prior art in its entirety (In re Bigio, In re Wesslau, Abbott Labs. v. Sandoz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement / prior art pertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference relied on as prior art must be analogous — either from the same field of endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem addressed by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the two tests from In re Bigio; challenge characterizations of references as prior art by arguing non-analogous nature, lack of enablement, incorrect priority date, or AIA vs pre-AIA differences. Cite MPEP § 2141.01(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be considered in its entirety (no picking-and-choosing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must consider each prior art reference in its entirety; it is impermissible to pick and choose isolated favorable portions while ignoring parts that teach away or otherwise discredit the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Wesslau, Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind/Hydrocurve, and Impax Labs. v. Lannett. Highlight portions of the reference that lead away from the asserted combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness must be judged with respect to the claimed invention as a whole, not by focusing on isolated differences or dissecting the invention part-by-part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue against inquiries that focus on individual aspects; cite MPEP § 2141.02 and cases (Jones v. Hardy; Ruiz v. A.B. Chance; Princeton Biochemicals; Allergan v. Apotex). Also ensure inherent properties of claims are considered (In re Antonie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner ignored a claim limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art or combination does not disclose one or more claim limitations, a rejection is improper — all claim limitations must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out omitted limitations and argue the examiner improperly overlooked them. Cite MPEP § 2143.03 and supporting case law (Medrad, Kinetic Concepts). Show that absent disclosure of a limitation, rejection cannot stand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge that the number of predictable solutions was finite
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the examiner relies on an inference that the claimed invention was one of a finite number of predictable solutions, an applicant can challenge that the range of predictable solutions was not finite and that choices were numerous and uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the multiplicity of choices and unpredictability, using cases like Eisai and Ortho-McNeil. Show steps a POSITA would have to take and uncertainties at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to show a reasonable motivation to combine or modify prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must show that a person of ordinary skill would have been reasonably motivated to combine or modify the cited prior art to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge asserted motivation by arguing (a) no basis for modification in prior art, (b) modification renders art inoperable, (c) prior art did not recognize the problem/solution, (d) prior art teaches away, (e) prosecution history rebuts motivation, or (f) examiner mischaracterized POSITA knowledge. Cite In re Lee; W.L. Gore; In re Dow Chem.; Cardiac Pacemakers; In re NTP; MPEP § 2143.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art or other evidence did not provide a basis for the proposed modification (hindsight problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion of obviousness cannot be based on using the applicant’s disclosure as a blueprint or on hindsight; there must be a reason/suggestion in the prior art for selecting the asserted modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-part 'lead compound' or analogous inquiries (e.g., Otsuka, Grain Processing) to show that prior art would not have led a POSITA to the claimed solution absent hindsight. Cite In re Dow Chem., Cardiac Pacemakers, In re NTP, and MPEP § 2143.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed modification renders the prior art inoperable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner’s proposed modification would make the prior art inoperable for its intended purpose or require substantial reconstruction, then there was no motivation to make the modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the asserted combination requires redesign or destroys intended function; cite In re Fritch, In re Ratti, In re Gordon, and MPEP § 2143.01(V)-(VI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art did not recognize the unsolved problem or suggest the solution
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner cannot infer motivation to combine references if the prior art did not recognize the problem the inventor solved or did not suggest the claimed solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that recognition of a need does not render the particular solution obvious (Cardiac Pacemakers v. St. Jude); show the references address different problems and that combining them is not suggested. Cite Broadcom v. Emulex, Insite Vision v. Sandoz, and Monarch Knitting precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art teaches away from the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior art would have led a POSITA in a different direction or discouraged the approach used by the inventor, that is strong evidence of nonobviousness (teaching away).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate clear discouragement or that the prior art would not have reasonably expected success. Note that 'teaching away' is a high bar and mere disclosure of alternatives is insufficient. Cite MPEP § 2143(E), In re Gurley, In re Fulton, Syntex v. Apotex, W.L. Gore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history of cited prior art rebuts motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution history of a cited patent or application may show that its own prosecution counselled against the combination asserted by the examiner, undermining the motivation-to-combine assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review file history of cited references for arguments, amendments, or declarations showing noninterchangeability or specific critical selections (example: Cohen/Holden prosecution history discussed). Use as evidence to rebut motivation to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner’s position on state of POSITA knowledge may be incorrect
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s characterization of what a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known or been motivated to do may be factually incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider submitting declarations, talking to authors (as in Louvel/Munsat example), or other contemporaneous evidence to correct the record on POSITA knowledge at the relevant time. Use to rebut examiner assertions about expectations of success or customary practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper application of 'obvious to try' post-KSR
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'obvious to try' conclusion is only appropriate where there was a design need/market pressure and a finite number of identified, predictable solutions such that a POSITA would have had good reason to pursue known options with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish circumstances where numerous unpredictable choices existed or where prior art gave no direction as to critical parameters. Cite KSR, Pfizer v. Apotex, In re Kubin, Leo Pharma, Eisai, and MPEP § 2143(I)(E). Require the examiner to articulate why a POSITA would have had a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reasonable expectation of success in combining/modifying prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires not only a motivation/suggestion but also a reasonable expectation of success; lack of such expectation undermines an obviousness finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for conflicts in teachings, submit evidence (declarations/experimental data) showing lack of expectation of success, and highlight unpredictability in the art. Cite In re Dow Chem., In re Clinton, In re Rinehart, Amgen v. Chugai, and UCB v. Accord. Beware of declaration pitfalls (timing, Rule 56, prosecution history estoppel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of declarations and data to rebut prima facie case (evidentiary practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may submit declarations or data during prosecution to show unpredictability or lack of reasonable expectation of success, but such submissions must be carefully planned and meet duty-of-candor obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit declarations early if needed to undermine a prima facie case, but ensure quality and consistency to avoid harm (see K-40 Electronics IPR example). Consider that declarations can create prosecution history estoppel and must respect Rule 56.
